prompt: How many megabytes is one write-ahead log segment on a default PostgreSQL server?
hint: ls -l printed 16777216 bytes.

prompt: What does `pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), :'before')` measure after an UPDATE?
hint: An LSN is a byte position.

choices.text: How many rows the UPDATE changed
choices.why: UPDATE reports that itself, 50000. The difference is in bytes of log.

choices.text: How many segments were archived in between
choices.why: Nothing was being archived yet; and the result is in bytes, not segments.

choices.text: The bytes of log written in between
choices.why: Right. Two positions in the log subtract to the amount of log written between them.

choices.text: How long the UPDATE took, in microseconds
choices.why: LSNs are positions, not times.

prompt: Updating every row of a table of about 3 MB wrote 15 MB of log. Which explains most of the difference?
hint: What does the first change to a page after a checkpoint log?

choices.text: Whole pages, logged on first change after a checkpoint
choices.why: Right. Full-page images and new index entries for each new row version add up to several times the data.

choices.text: The log stores every row twice, once for safety
choices.why: There is no duplicate copy for safety; each change is logged once, in its own form.

choices.text: The log is uncompressed text, much larger than the table's binary format
choices.why: The log is binary records, not text.

choices.text: The UPDATE ran twice because of a retry
choices.why: UPDATE 50000 ran once.

prompt: What does `SELECT pg_switch_wal()` do?
hint: The segment does not have to be full.

choices.text: It moves the log to a different directory
choices.why: The directory stays pg_wal; only the segment being written changes.

choices.text: It turns archiving on without a restart
choices.why: archive_mode still needs a restart; the switch only closes a segment.

choices.text: It deletes the segments the server no longer needs
choices.why: Recycling happens at checkpoints, not on a switch.

choices.text: It finishes the current segment now and starts the next one
choices.why: Right. That is how this lesson makes a segment available to the archive without waiting for it to fill.

prompt: Match each setting or placeholder with what it does.
hint: One of them needs a restart.

pairs.right: Makes the server track which segments have been archived; changing it needs a restart
The shell command run once for each finished segment
Replaced by the path of the segment to archive
Replaced by the segment's file name alone

right_distractors: Closes a segment after a set time if anything was written to it

prompt: Why does the archive command start with `test ! -f /var/lib/postgresql/wal-archive/%f &&`?
hint: What should happen if a segment with that name is already archived?

choices.text: To make the copy faster when the file already exists
choices.why: It does not copy faster; it refuses to copy at all if the file exists.

choices.text: Never overwriting an archived segment
choices.why: Right. Another server archiving into the same place would otherwise replace your history silently.

choices.text: Because cp cannot create files in an empty directory
choices.why: cp creates files in empty directories without trouble.

choices.text: To skip segments that have not been written yet
choices.why: The server only calls the command for finished segments; there is nothing to skip.

prompt: The lesson calls `cp` the simplest archive command that works and not a good one for production. What is its weakness?
hint: When does cp report success?

choices.text: It cannot copy files of 16 MB
choices.why: It copied 16 MB without trouble.

choices.text: It says done before the bytes are on disk
choices.why: Right: success before the copy is known to be on disk. A power cut a moment later can lose a segment the server believes is archived, and then recycles.

choices.text: It does not keep the file's permissions
choices.why: Permissions are not what makes an archive safe.

choices.text: It runs as ana instead of postgres
choices.why: The server runs it, as postgres.

prompt: The archive directory becomes unwritable. What do the application's queries notice?
hint: Where does the failure show up?

choices.text: Every write fails until archiving is fixed
choices.why: Writes carry on; the server keeps the segments and retries.

choices.text: Commits slow down while the server retries
choices.why: Archiving happens in its own process, after commit; commits are not delayed by it.

choices.text: The database switches to read-only
choices.why: It does not, until the disk holding pg_wal is full, when it stops altogether.

choices.text: Nothing; a log line and a counter show it
choices.why: Right. That is correct behaviour and exactly what makes the failure dangerous.

prompt: With the archive broken, how many segments were waiting as `.ready` after six more updates?
hint: grep -c counted them.

prompt: A broken archive command goes unnoticed for long enough that the disk holding `pg_wal` fills. What happens to the database?
hint: What can a server not do without writing to its log?

choices.text: It cannot write the log, so it stops accepting writes and shuts down
choices.why: Right. A backup problem nobody saw becomes an outage everybody sees.

choices.text: It deletes the oldest unarchived segments to make room
choices.why: It never throws away log it has not archived; that would break the backup silently.

choices.text: It stops archiving and carries on
choices.why: Archiving already failed. The problem is that it cannot write new log.

choices.text: It moves pg_wal to another disk automatically
choices.why: There is no such mechanism.

prompt: A database writes 2 GB of log an hour. Its archive breaks at 18:00 on Friday and nobody notices until 06:00 on Monday. About how many GB of segments has the server kept by then?
hint: Count the hours.

prompt: After the fix, `failed_count` still reads 13. A monitoring rule alerts when `failed_count > 0`. What is wrong with the rule?
hint: What does the counter count?

choices.text: Nothing: 13 failures is worth an alert
choices.why: They are old failures, already recovered from. The alert would fire for ever.

choices.text: failed_count only counts segments that were finally archived
choices.why: It counts failed attempts, whether or not the segment was archived later.

choices.text: It counts old attempts too, so it never clears
choices.why: Right: it counts attempts since the last reset, so one incident keeps it above zero for ever. Compare it with its previous value, and watch last_archived_time and the .ready files too.

choices.text: It should alert on archived_count instead
choices.why: archived_count going up says things work; it cannot say something failed.

prompt: On a quiet server with no `archive_timeout`, an order is written into a segment that is far from full. When is it archived?
hint: A segment is archived when it is finished.

choices.text: Within a second, because the order committed
choices.why: Committing writes the log to the server's own disk. Archiving waits for the segment to finish.

choices.text: At the next checkpoint
choices.why: Checkpoints do not finish segments; they make old ones recyclable.

choices.text: Never, because a partial segment cannot be archived
choices.why: It is archived once something finishes it, by filling or by a switch.

choices.text: When the segment fills, days later on a quiet server
choices.why: Right. Until then the order exists only on the server.

prompt: What does `archive_timeout = '60s'` do on a server where nothing has been written for an hour?
hint: It only closes a segment if anything was written to it.

choices.text: Archives an empty segment every minute
choices.why: It closes a segment only if something was written to it, so an idle server produces nothing.

choices.text: Stops the archiver until something is written
choices.why: The archiver keeps running; there is just nothing to hand it.

choices.text: Nothing: no change to close a segment for
choices.why: Right. It bounds how long a change waits, and costs nothing when there are no changes.

choices.text: Forces a checkpoint every minute
choices.why: archive_timeout switches segments; it does not cause checkpoints.

prompt: Segment `0D` held one order and had been open for more than a minute when `archive_timeout = '60s'` was set and reloaded. What did the server do?
hint: The timeout was already exceeded.

choices.text: Closed 0D at once, so the next order went into 0E
choices.why: Right. 0D was archived straight away, and 0E sixty seconds later.

choices.text: Waited sixty seconds from the reload, then closed 0D
choices.why: The minute is measured from when the segment was last switched, which was already more than a minute ago.

choices.text: Nothing until 0D filled, because a timeout only applies to new segments
choices.why: The setting applied at once to the open segment.

choices.text: Discarded 0D, because it was nearly empty
choices.why: Nothing is discarded. An almost empty segment is archived like any other.

prompt: A server writes something every minute and has `archive_timeout = '60s'`. Each closed segment is 16 MB. Roughly how many GB of archive does a day add, before compression?
hint: 1440 minutes in a day.

prompt: Why was the file `pg_receivewal` wrote called `…0F.partial`?
hint: Is segment 0F finished?

choices.text: Because the copy failed halfway
choices.why: Nothing failed. The server has not finished writing that segment.

choices.text: Because the server is still writing that segment
choices.why: Right. It is renamed without the suffix once the segment is finished.

choices.text: Because pg_receivewal compresses part of each file
choices.why: No compression was asked for, and the suffix is not about it.

choices.text: Because the slot only allows partial copies
choices.why: The slot keeps log for the receiver; it does not limit what is sent.

prompt: A `pg_receivewal` was stopped and its slot left in place, `active` false. What does the slot do from then on?
hint: Look at restart_lsn.

choices.text: Nothing: an inactive slot is ignored
choices.why: An inactive slot is the dangerous kind: it keeps its promise with nobody to collect.

choices.text: It disappears after archive_timeout
choices.why: Slots never expire on their own here; somebody has to drop them.

choices.text: Keep every segment from restart_lsn on
choices.why: Right: the server keeps every segment from the slot's restart_lsn onwards. With no receiver, that pile grows until somebody drops the slot or the disk fills.

choices.text: It forces every segment to be archived twice
choices.why: It keeps segments on the server; it does not touch the archive.

prompt: With a streaming receiver running, how much log can be lost if the primary's disk dies?
hint: Does the server wait for the receiver before a commit returns?

choices.text: The last fraction of a second
choices.why: Right. Small and not zero.

choices.text: A whole segment, as with archive_command
choices.why: The receiver has the log as it is written, not only when a segment ends.

choices.text: Up to archive_timeout
choices.why: That is the bound for an archive command on a quiet server.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: A commit returns before the receiver has the record, unless the server is made to wait (lesson 12).

prompt: Base backups are taken every Sunday and the last four are kept. From when must the archive be kept?
hint: Recovery starts from a base backup and needs every segment after its start.

choices.text: From the start of the newest base backup
choices.why: Then the three older base backups could not be brought forward to any point.

choices.text: For the last seven days only
choices.why: Seven days covers one backup, not four.

choices.text: Only from the last checkpoint
choices.why: Checkpoints decide what the server needs for crash recovery, not what a backup needs.

choices.text: From the oldest kept backup's start
choices.why: Right. Restoring from the oldest needs every segment from its start point onwards.

prompt: A segment from Wednesday is missing from the archive; everything else from Sunday's base backup to Friday is there. A restore is needed to Friday 15:00. How far can it go from Sunday's backup?
hint: Replay is a chain.

choices.text: To Friday 15:00, skipping the missing segment
choices.why: Replay cannot skip: every record depends on the ones before it.

choices.text: Up to where the missing segment begins
choices.why: Right. Recovery stops at the first gap, however much archive comes after it.

choices.text: Only to the end of the base backup on Sunday
choices.why: Monday and Tuesday are unbroken and replay through them.

choices.text: Nowhere, the whole archive is invalid
choices.why: Everything before the gap is usable.

prompt: Put what a recovery to a moment after the base backup needs, in the order it uses them.
hint: Start from the copy of the files.
items: Its backup_label, saying where replay starts
Every archived segment from there, without a gap
trap: The label points into the log; the segments are replayed in order from there; and replay stops at the chosen moment, which lesson 6 sets.

prompt: You inherit a server whose `pg_stat_archiver` shows `archived_count` 50211, `failed_count` 0 and `last_archived_time` three days ago. The database is busy. What is happening?
hint: A busy server finishes segments every few minutes.

choices.text: Everything is fine: no failures
choices.why: No failures and no archiving for three days on a busy server is a command that hangs instead of failing.

choices.text: Archiving has stalled without failing, and pg_wal is filling
choices.why: Right. That is why last_archived_time and the .ready count are alerted on, not only failures.

choices.text: The server is idle, so there was nothing to archive
choices.why: The question says it is busy.

choices.text: archive_mode was switched off three days ago
choices.why: Then the statistics would have been reset by the restart, and pg_wal would not be the risk.
